meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

watches.desc: Watches follow one thread of an item on its own once a trigger event makes it worth it: an information-operations watch (kind "info-ops": official messaging, state-media narratives and documented influence campaigns), a shadow-war watch (kind "shadow-war": sabotage, incursions, cyber and influence below the threshold of war, and the targeted side's responses) or an operation watch (kind "operation": one named military operation, its gains, the enemy's response and what it shows). Each carries a narrower daily feed, plus dated findings and an assessment researched from open sources at each review.

types.official statement: Government, foreign-ministry, military or party statement aimed at an audience (strategic communications).
types.state-media narrative: Framing pushed by state or party media, including English-language outlets aimed abroad.
types.covert information operation: Documented coordinated inauthentic behaviour, disinformation or cognitive-warfare activity, attributed by a credible reporter.
types.coercive signalling: Military, coast-guard or legal action whose purpose is the message it sends.
types.sanctions/lawfare: Sanctions, lists or legal framing used to pressure or delegitimise.
types.counter-messaging: The targeted side's official response or rebuttal.
types.domestic narrative: Narratives inside the targeted polity (parties, polls, viral claims).
types.debunked claim: A specific false claim identified by a fact-checker.
types.third-party assessment: Analysis by a think-tank, researcher or major outlet.
types.hybrid attack: Physical sabotage, arson, cable or pipeline damage, cyber attacks, GPS jamming, drone or airspace incursions and other deniable attacks below the threshold of war.
types.defensive response: The targeted side's practical countermeasures: arrests, expulsions, airspace closures, deployments, new laws and alliance consultations.
types.territorial change: Ground or settlements gained or lost, with who reports it and whether it is independently confirmed (geolocated footage, ISW).
types.official claim: A command's or ministry's claim of gains, enemy losses or prisoners that has not been independently confirmed.
types.counterattack: The opposing side's counterattacks, reinforcements or renewed assaults in the operation's sector.
types.tactic or capability: A tactic, weapon or enabler used in the operation (drones, electronic warfare, converted vehicles, shaping strikes).

items.whyNow: Russia is hitting Ukraine's grid daily (more than 170 energy strikes since 11 Oct) and used cluster-warhead Iskanders on central Kyiv on 22 Oct while talks restart, and Ukraine's air defence and drone war hinge on US-controlled enablers (Starlink speed caps, 12 Patriot interceptors a month); it is the clearest live test of how layered air defence, dispersed repair and drone-led offensives cope when key enablers are throttled.
changes: 22 Oct: Russia struck Kyiv with three cluster-warhead ballistic missiles, one landing in historic Pechersk, with at least four killed and 34 wounded; Zelensky counted over 170 energy strikes since 11 Oct, and Trump reportedly asked Musk to lift Starlink speed caps (WSJ via Reuters) (Ukrinform, Jerusalem Post/Reuters).

21 Oct: Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg; Putin said the Oslo proposals held "little that was useful" and Peskov said Russia needs "peace, not a ceasefire", but Ushakov said Moscow is in principle ready for trilateral talks around 10 Nov, possibly in Abu Dhabi, as Russia freed US citizen Stephen Hubbard and readied a first diesel tanker for the US (ISW).

20 Oct: Zelensky met Witkoff and European leaders in Oslo after a call with Rubio on interceptors, intelligence and Starlink, and said early-warning intelligence sharing "is now working"; Ukraine hit an oil pumping station in Tambov Oblast (Al Jazeera, ISW).

19 Oct: Biletskyi said Operation Vivaldi reached the Zherebets River and defeated Russia's northern pincer on Lyman, as ISW assessed Ukrainian advances near Myrne and Zarichne; overnight 16 ballistic missiles and over 200 drones hit Kyiv region and 28 energy sites, leaving 550,000 households without power, and Zelensky said the US supplies only 12 Patriot interceptors a month (ISW).

18 Oct: Ukraine launched over 1,000 drones at Russia (Russian MoD count), setting fire to the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and Ruchi depot and hitting a VK data centre about 850 km from the border, while Ukraine imposed nationwide power limitation schedules after Russian substation strikes (TNND, ISW).

17 Oct: Romanian F-16s shot down two jet-powered Geran drones near Sulina, a first for Romania, after Trump signed an order on 16 Oct waiving key Russia sanctions; Zelensky said a 100 mph Starlink speed cap cuts Ukrainian drones off (ISW).

next.text: Whether US–Ukraine–Russia trilateral talks actually resume around 10 Nov (possibly Abu Dhabi) as Ushakov said on 21 Oct, and whether Moscow moves from rejecting the Oslo proposals and any energy ceasefire.
next.ifSeen: Talks convene with an energy or air truce on the table → phase check and flag today; postponed or Russia keeps rejecting → track only.

next.text: Starlink speed caps (160 km/h) fully lifted after Trump's reported 22 Oct call to Musk, and whether Ukraine's interception rate against jet-powered drones (54% in September) and its intermediate-range drone strikes recover.
next.ifSeen: Caps lifted with rising jet-drone interception → note for the monthly pattern set; caps persist or are reimposed → escalate.

next.text: Patriot interceptor supply above the 12 a month Zelensky cited on 19 Oct (PURL deliveries unblocked), versus further ballistic salvos of 15 or more missiles, including cluster-warhead Iskanders, on Kyiv with few interceptions.
next.ifSeen: Larger deliveries confirmed → note for the monthly pattern set; another large salvo largely unintercepted → escalate.

next.text: Nationwide power limitation schedules imposed on 18 Oct still in force in November, or a single strike again leaving 500,000+ households without power (550,000 on 19 Oct).
next.ifSeen: Escalate; restoration hours and repair throughput become the metric for dispersed support under repeated targeting.

next.text: ISW or geolocated confirmation of Ukrainian advances beyond the Zherebets River line (Yampolivka, Terny, Ivanivka) claimed on 19 Oct, versus Russian consolidation in Dobropillia or on the T-0514 Dobropillia–Kramatorsk highway reported by Mashovets on 21 Oct.
next.ifSeen: Confirmed Ukrainian gains → phase check on an operational-level shift; Russian consolidation in Dobropillia → escalate.

next.text: A Russian decree for an involuntary reservist call-up, which ISW (20 Oct) reports Putin is reluctantly considering, or verified arrival of North Korean troops at the front.
next.ifSeen: Decree or verified North Korean deployment → escalate and phase check; covert regional call-ups only → note for the monthly pattern set.

timeline.text: Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

A daylight Russian jet-drone raid hit Kyiv's National Academy of Sciences and killed five people across Ukraine, Zelensky said Russia had begun additional mobilisation as Putin enlarged the armed forces by 15,500, and the 3rd Army Corps closed Vivaldi's third stage with 51 square kilometres, three settlements and over 250 prisoners taken using converted BTR-60s as kamikaze vehicles.

Russian drones struck Kyiv's Southern Bridge while a metro train was crossing, the first attack on a Kyiv bridge of the full-scale war, as Ukraine reported the first combat use of its FP-7 ballistic missile.
On Putin's birthday Russia fired 48 cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and 130 drones across Ukraine, killing at least 30 people, more than 20 of them in an apartment block in Pryluky.
Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire that neither Kyiv nor Moscow had confirmed, and Russian forces struck the Kharkiv thermal power plant hours later.

Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones at energy sites around Kyiv and Kharkiv, leaving 600,000 without power, as the 3rd Army Corps claimed a fourth Vivaldi stage of 101 square kilometres north of Lyman.

Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting fires at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and Ruchi depot and hitting a VK data centre about 850 km from the border, its deepest mass raid of the war.

Hours after Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg, Russia hit Kyiv with three cluster-warhead ballistic missiles, one landing between the Pechersk Lavra and a monastery, killing at least four and wounding 34.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status holds and still favours Ukraine north of Lyman: on 19 Oct Biletskyi said Operation Vivaldi reached the Zherebets River and defeated Russia's northern pincer, and on 21 Oct ISW credited it with at least 277 sq km, while Russian infiltration produced only a flag-raising in Dobropillia on 18 Oct that ISW could not confirm as consolidation. Cosmos-2612 closing to 26 metres of a Finnish SAR satellite on 19 Oct shows the contest reaching space-based imagery. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising status is borne out, but the binding constraint is access to enablers rather than jamming: the 160 km/h Starlink cap still disrupted interceptor-drone links on 19–20 Oct and, per Unmanned Systems Forces data cited by ISW, degraded intermediate-range strikes, until Trump reportedly asked Musk to lift it on 22 Oct.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status hardens on both sides. Russia hit 28 energy sites on 18–19 Oct, cutting power to 550,000 households and forcing nationwide limitation schedules, then used cluster-warhead Iskanders on Kyiv on 22 Oct; Ukraine's 1,000-drone raid on St Petersburg fuel and data nodes on 18 Oct mirrors the method. Repair throughput, not protection, remains decisive.

status.summary: The week's most significant developments were Ukraine's 1,000-drone raid on St Petersburg's oil terminal and a VK data centre on 18 Oct, Russia's strikes on 28 energy sites that left 550,000 households without power on 19 Oct, and a diplomatic push in which Witkoff met Zelensky and Europeans in Oslo on 20 Oct and Putin on 21 Oct, after which Russia hit Kyiv with cluster-warhead ballistic missiles on 22 Oct while agreeing in principle to trilateral talks around 10 Nov. Over the week the strike war on both sides' energy and infrastructure escalated further and US enablers (Starlink caps, a 12-a-month Patriot supply, sanctions waivers) remained the main friction, while on the ground Ukraine extended its gains north of Lyman to the Zherebets River and Russian infiltration of Dobropillia stayed unconsolidated.

findings.actor: German Federal Prosecutor's Office (GBA)
findings.text: On 22 Oct 2026 German federal prosecutors had a Ukrainian national, Vadym Y., arrested in Brandenburg on suspicion of gathering information for a Russian intelligence service on armoured-vehicle, ammunition and explosives production and on sites securing NATO's eastern flank, partly by approaching defence-industry staff. The arrest worked as an interdiction, but prosecutors allege he had been in contact with Russian intelligence through an intermediary since at least July 2025, so the collection ran for about 15 months before it was stopped.

findings.actor: Bundeswehr Operational Command
findings.tactic: Raising sabotage threat level, hardening bases
findings.text: Defense News reported on 21 Oct 2026 that the Bundeswehr had raised its Russian sabotage threat assessment to the second-highest level, triggered by a crashed drone found with a can of explosives near Wunstorf air base and by suspicious drone overflights of Arrow 3 and Patriot sites. The assessment says vulnerable sites can no longer be confined geographically and that drone use has crossed a red line toward lethal effects; protective measures are being strengthened at installations, but none has yet been tested against an attack.

findings.actor: Russian fishing trawlers (per a Telegraph data investigation)
findings.text: A Telegraph analysis of 4.5 years of Global Fishing Watch data, published on 21 Oct 2026 and relayed by UNITED24 on 22 Oct, found 17 Russian trawlers making more than 500 slow, suspicious movements over North Atlantic cables, including 337 hours over Atlantic Crossing 1 north of Scotland. An unnamed NATO official said some ships may not be fishing at all; the data do not prove espionage or any damage, and the reporting names no countermeasure (single source).

findings.actor: North Atlantic Council
findings.tactic: Surveillance surge after Black Sea ship strikes
findings.text: After the North Atlantic Council met on 20 Oct 2026, NATO said allies had sent or would send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radars, explosive-exploitation teams, intelligence personnel and drones to the Black Sea following the drone strikes on merchant ships off Romania and Bulgaria. The priority is better situational awareness rather than interception, and NATO still did not name a perpetrator, so whether the deployment deters further strikes is untested.

findings.actor: Unidentified arsonists (Lithuanian PM: commissioned by Russia); Lithuanian authorities
findings.tactic: Arson on Starlink sites serving Ukraine
findings.text: At about 02:00 on 18 Oct 2026 attackers tried to burn satellite antennas and a control unit at a Lithuanian firm providing connectivity for Starlink antennas used by Ukraine; incendiary liquids in 3-10 litre containers were found. The attempt failed because authorities had warned the company and security had been stepped up, a rare case of pre-emptive warning stopping the arson pattern seen in Poland and Bulgaria. PM Sinkevičius blamed Russia without presenting proof, and a pre-trial investigation is open.

findings.actor: Romanian Air Force
findings.text: On the evening of 17 Oct 2026 two Romanian F-16s scrambled from Borcea after radar detected several targets and shot down two drones over territorial waters near Sulina, the first within about two minutes of entering Romanian airspace and the second at 18:05. The Defence Ministry identified them as jet-powered Geran-family attack drones; it is a clear interception success, though their launch point and target were not stated.

findings.actor: Unidentified drones (ISW: likely Russian); Moldovan air surveillance
findings.tactic: Repeated drone overflights of northern Moldova
findings.text: ISW reported that on 15-16 Oct 2026 at least four drones violated Moldovan airspace at least five times and that one crashed and exploded near Scaieni, Donduseni district, about 30 km inside Moldova. Moldova's air surveillance recorded the violations this time, an improvement on the undetected 10 Oct incursion, but nothing was intercepted; Moldova's MoD did not attribute the drones, which ISW assesses were likely Russian.

findings.actor: Unidentified drone operators (ISW: likely Russian); Bulgarian government
findings.tactic: Drone strikes on merchant ships in EEZ
findings.text: Early on 13 Oct 2026 drones hit the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3 about 18 nautical miles off Bulgaria and sank the cargo ship HS Dignity off Krapets, leaving 11 crew missing, a week after a 6 Oct strike in the same zone that sank a ship. Nothing was intercepted; Sofia summoned Russia's ambassador and asked NATO and the EU for help, but did not formally attribute the attack, and ISW assessed Russia is extending risk-taking from airspace incursions to maritime strikes.

findings.actor: French Navy
findings.text: On 12 Oct 2026 the French Navy boarded the sanctioned tanker DF Peak more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion on suspicion of a false Benin flag, and is escorting it for inspection; it is at least the fifth Russia-linked tanker France has stopped since 2024. The boarding worked as an interdiction, but no confiscation or criminal liability has yet been established, and Moscow called it piracy.

findings.actor: Polish ABW and police with German BKA
findings.text: On 12 Oct 2026 two Turkish men were detained in Nürtingen, Germany, at Poland's request over the 23 Sep arson at an Exatel Starlink ground station near Warsaw; Poland said it had recordings, fingerprints and DNA and had "no doubt" Russian services were behind it. The cell was identified within three weeks and faces sabotage charges, but the attack itself was not prevented and Poland says others were likely involved.

findings.actor: Moldovan air surveillance against an unidentified strike drone
findings.text: On the night of 10 Oct 2026 a drone carrying an explosive payload crashed into a tree near Geamăna, Anenii Noi district, about 20 km inside Moldova; police neutralised the warhead and no one was hurt. Moldova's Defence Ministry said its air surveillance had recorded no unauthorised flight, so the incursion went undetected; Chisinau did not attribute it, while ISW judged it likely Russian and part of a normalising pattern.

findings.actor: Two 19-year-old German nationals (Bulgaria has not named a sponsor); Bulgarian prosecutors
findings.text: On 9 Oct 2026 two men set fire to antennas at the Plana teleport near Sofia, a Starlink site used in part by Ukraine. Bulgarian prosecutors charged two German nationals in absentia on 14 Oct and a Sofia court cleared European arrest warrants, but both had already left Bulgaria and remained at large as of 20 Oct, so the attack achieved its effect and the perpetrators escaped; Bulgaria has not attributed it to Russia.

assessment.text: Between 9 and 22 Oct 2026 Russia's cheapest deniable tools kept working where defenders lacked warning. Drones crossed northern Moldova repeatedly on 15-16 Oct, one exploding near Scaieni, and two arsonists burned Bulgaria's Plana Starlink teleport on 9 Oct and left the country before they were charged. Countermeasures improved where prepared. Romanian F-16s downed two jet-powered Geran drones near Sulina within minutes on 17 Oct, and a forewarned Lithuanian firm defeated an arson attempt on its Starlink equipment on 18 Oct, breaking the run of successful Starlink arsons. Germany arrested an alleged defence-industry spy on 22 Oct after some 15 months of activity. Defenders are shifting from reacting to hardening: NATO's 20 Oct Black Sea surveillance surge and the Bundeswehr's raised threat level of 21 Oct. Neither is yet tested, attribution is still withheld at sea, and trawler loitering over cables remains legal and unremedied (single source).

watches.trigger: 3rd Army Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi reveals Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive north of Lyman, 15 Sep 2026
watches.question: Can Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, the 3rd Army Corps counteroffensive north of Lyman, keep regaining ground and disrupt Russia's planned pincer on the Donbas fortress belt (Lyman–Sviatohirsk in the north, Dobropillia in the south, converging on Barvinkove), how is Russia responding with counterattacks, reserves and narrative, and what does it show about restoring manoeuvre under drone-saturated conditions?

findings.actor: Russian command (50th Varyag Unmanned Systems Brigade)
findings.tactic: Redeploying an elite drone brigade to Lyman
findings.text: Militarnyi reported on 22 Oct 2026 that part of Russia's 50th Varyag Unmanned Systems Brigade had been moved to the Lyman area to stabilise the front, based on an analyst's reading of a Russian video showing a drone hitting a 3rd Army Corps ground robot. It replaces the Rubicon Center, which Russia withdrew from the Lyman-Borova axis to reconstitute after losses the corps claims it inflicted, so one drone formation has been superseded by another; the redeployment rests on a single video (single source).

findings.actor: 3rd Army Corps assault infantry
findings.text: A Kyiv Independent field report of 22 Oct 2026 described pairs and small groups infiltrating up to 5 km behind Russian lines to cut supply routes and block retreats, varying routes and timings, and encircling Shandryholove along treelines instead of storming it. A battalion commander reported minimal casualties, though 30-40% of teams were spotted by drones; the outcome rests on the units' accounts, consistent with the corps' declared 277 km² and 16 settlements by 14 Oct.

findings.actor: Russian forces in the Lyman sector
findings.text: The same 22 Oct 2026 Kyiv Independent report said anti-personnel mines caused about 80% of one unit's casualties, turned back two groups at a river crossing and hit evacuation teams, while a six-man assault faced about 35 fibre-optic FPVs and 12 Molniya drones in two hours and ground robots were prime targets. These barriers slowed advances to as little as 200 m in four days but did not stop the operation.

findings.actor: 3rd Army Corps middle-strike drone units
findings.text: Euromaidan Press argued on 22 Oct 2026 that Starlink/Starshield command links and middle-strike drones hitting Russian supply lines were pivotal to Vivaldi, but that a speed cap in force since 14 Oct cuts terminals on drones flying faster than about 160 km/h. A commentator citing Russian sources says Ukrainian deep strikes have fallen significantly; no Russian ground regained has been documented, so the method is degraded rather than defeated (single source).

findings.actor: Russian 25th Combined Arms Army
findings.tactic: Assaults east of Lyman near Zarichne
findings.text: ISW reported that Russian forces concentrated attacks east of Lyman near Zarichne on 20 and 21 Oct 2026 but did not advance. ISW's 18 Oct report likewise showed a geolocated Russian infiltration on Lyman's eastern outskirts without any confirmed advance, and ISW now states that Vivaldi defeated the northern pincer of the planned encirclement.

findings.actor: 1030th Air Defence Regiment 'Aquila' interceptor battalion (3rd Army Corps)
findings.text: Euromaidan Press, citing ArmyInform on 21 Oct 2026, reported the battalion's claim to have destroyed several thousand Russian aerial targets during Vivaldi, including Zala, Orlan and Supercam reconnaissance drones. Against jet-powered Shaheds, however, interceptors scored only small numbers because they need 500-600 km/h, and the regiment still relies mainly on guns and SAMs for them.

findings.actor: Ukrainian forces north and east of Lyman
findings.tactic: Pushing to the Zherebets River line
findings.text: ISW's 19 Oct 2026 assessment cited observer Kostyantyn Mashovets that Ukrainian forces had likely pushed Russian troops out of Myrne, reached the Zherebets south of Torske and Myrne and advanced into northern Zarichne, while Russian milbloggers claimed to have lost and retaken positions in southern Zarichne. These gains are not geolocated, and some Russian assault groups still hold positions in the Stavky-Kolodyazi-Myrne-Zarichne area.

findings.actor: Russian 144th Motorized Rifle Division (20th Combined Arms Army)
findings.text: Biletskyi said on 19 Oct 2026 that the 144th Division, which formed much of the grouping on the Chornyi Zherebets bridgehead, had in effect ceased to exist as an organised force, the bridgehead was eliminated and Russia had temporarily dropped its plan to reach Barvinkove via Sviatohirsk. The degradation is a Ukrainian claim, but ISW on 20 Oct judged Russia would have to reconstitute the division before any new Lyman offensive.

findings.actor: 3rd Army Corps drone and mechanized units
findings.tactic: Drone close air support for encirclement
findings.text: ISW's 18 Oct 2026 report relayed a Ukrainian drone battalion officer's account that drones escorted infantry in missions akin to close air support and that mechanized forces encircled Kolodyazi and took it without urban combat; on 17 Oct a brigade said forward-deployed drone teams reached Russian armour previously out of range and a drone unit hit a TOS-3 over 12 km behind the line. The accounts are the units' own, but Kolodyazi's capture is consistent with ISW's reporting.

findings.actor: 3rd Army Corps deception unit
findings.tactic: Dedicated deception feeding false battlefield picture
findings.text: UNITED24 reported on 15 Oct 2026 that the corps ran a dedicated unit that fed Russian forces, including higher command, a deliberately false picture of the battlefield, alongside suicide ground robots used behind Russian lines. The corps credits this with surprise and with exhausting Russian reserves in its sector; the account is the corps' own and not independently confirmed.

findings.actor: 3rd Army Corps (Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi)
findings.text: On 14 Oct 2026 the corps said the fourth and final "season" of Vivaldi had retaken 101 km² including Zelena Dolyna, Lypove and Kolodiazi, for 277 km² and 16 settlements overall, and claimed about 3,000 Russian losses in the phase (8,000 in total, 250+ prisoners). The area and loss figures are claims; ISW's 13 Oct report placing Russian attacks "toward Kolodyazi" without gains is consistent with Ukrainian control, and Biletskyi said the operation continues in another form.

findings.actor: Russian command (1st Guards Tank Army, per Biletskyi)
findings.tactic: Shifting tank-army units from Kupiansk to Lyman
findings.text: Biletskyi said on 14 Oct 2026 that Vivaldi halted the Russian West grouping's offensive and forced some 1st Tank Army units to move from the Kupiansk direction to Lyman, easing pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi and securing the Kharkiv–Sloviansk highway. The redeployment did not stop the fourth-phase gains; the transfer itself is a Ukrainian claim not confirmed by ISW.

assessment.text: Vivaldi's methods kept paying off after the fourth phase ended on 14 Oct. Russian assaults near Zarichne on 20-21 Oct gained nothing, observers placed Ukrainian troops on the Zherebets and in northern Zarichne on 19 Oct (not geolocated), and ISW endorsed on 20 Oct the claim that the 144th Division must be rebuilt. Field accounts of 18 and 22 Oct credit small infiltration teams, drone close air support and encirclement over urban assault, while Russian mines and FPV saturation imposed most losses and slowed advances without stopping them. Russia is adapting with drones rather than infantry: the Varyag brigade has reportedly replaced the battered Rubicon Center around Lyman (22 Oct, single source). Ukraine's air-defence interceptors still cannot reliably catch jet-powered Shaheds (21 Oct). The Starshield speed cap in force since 14 Oct threatens the middle-strike interdiction that shaped the offensive, so the corps' new defensive posture is now contested on communications rather than on the ground.

items.whyNow: With the 27 Oct Israeli election days away, a reported IDF and Shin Bet assessment that only renewed fighting can disarm Hamas and an unusually explicit Hamas warning of new attacks have sharpened the choice between a renewed offensive and the stalled phase-two transition.
changes: 22 Oct: Haaretz reported an IDF and Shin Bet assessment, briefed to US officers and Israeli leaders, that Hamas has re-established its rule and can only be disarmed by renewed fighting, though no date or final plan exists; Ynet reported a Hamas warning of attacks inside Israel, the West Bank and abroad, relayed on 21 Oct through UN coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov to COGAT (single source, COGAT-confirmed to Ynet); far-right activists joined by MK Yulia Malinovsky blocked aid trucks at Kerem Shalom (Haaretz; Ynet; i24NEWS; Arab News).

22 Oct: Israeli fire killed four in 24 hours, including a girl near Jabalia and a man in a vehicle strike in Tal al-Hawa, taking deaths since the truce to 1,538, with nearly two-thirds of Gaza under Israeli control or access restrictions; the IDF said a 21 Oct strike in Khan Younis killed Ramadan Diab, head of the Popular Resistance Committees there (Al Jazeera; Jerusalem Post).

20 Oct: An air strike on a Rimal apartment near Shifa Hospital killed Akram Yassin, whom the IDF and Shin Bet called a senior officer of Hamas's leadership-protection general security apparatus, and his wife; Gaza civil defence reported seven killed that day and Al Jazeera put deaths since the truce at 1,522 (Times of Israel; Al Jazeera).

19 Oct: A strike in northern Gaza City killed Tamer al-Sabbagh, whom the IDF called the last surviving member of the cell filmed abducting Shani Louk's body on 7 Oct 2023, and two boys aged 13 and 14 were killed near Khan Younis; COGAT said private-sector goods would gradually resume after a halt from 13 Oct over Hamas levies on merchants that cut daily truck entries from about 600 to about 300 (Times of Israel; Al Jazeera).

18 Oct: The World Food Programme said funding shortfalls forced it to cut food assistance in Gaza from about 1.8 million people to about 500,000, during the commercial halt (Arab News; Times of Israel).

timeline.text: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the US Gaza plan, welcoming the Board of Peace and authorising an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.
Israel's security cabinet approved entry of an initial International Stabilization Force of about 200 personnel from countries such as Uganda and Morocco, operating in coordination with the IDF.

The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, while an Israeli strike in western Khan Younis killed senior Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven dead that day.

The Gaza Division commander said Israel controls 63% of Gaza with almost 40 new outposts, and the IDF published a list of 170 Palestinians reported as slain journalists whom it says belonged to armed groups.

On the first anniversary of the ceasefire Israeli attacks killed at least eight people across Gaza, including an eight-year-old girl, while no stabilisation force had deployed and the Palestinian technocratic committee was still kept out of the Strip.
Reports said Israel was still refusing entry to the US contractor hired to build the first base for Moroccan and Kosovan stabilisation troops, two months after the contract was awarded.
Israel said private-sector goods would gradually resume entering Gaza after a week-long halt, blamed on Hamas levies on merchants, that had cut daily truck entries from about 600 to about 300.

Israeli media reported a military intelligence assessment that Hamas can only be disarmed through renewed fighting, as a Hamas warning of new attacks inside Israel, the West Bank and abroad was relayed to Israel through the UN humanitarian coordinator.

text: On dense urban operations versus dispersed and concealed networks, the Established and Contested status is borne out: an IDF and Shin Bet assessment reported on 22 Oct holds that Hamas has re-established its rule and will only be disarmed by renewed ground fighting in areas troops have not entered, and a Hamas warning relayed on 21 Oct (single source) threatened attacks in Israel, the West Bank and abroad, so the network has reconstituted rather than been dismantled by strikes. On persistent ISR and precision strike versus civilian protection and legitimacy, the Contested status sharpens: strikes on 19 and 20 Oct killed the last surviving member of a 7 Oct abduction cell and a senior officer of Hamas's leadership-protection apparatus with his wife in a Rimal apartment, while two boys died near Khan Younis and deaths since the truce reached 1,538 by 22 Oct, so precise targeting of cadres continues to carry visible civilian cost.

On humanitarian access versus operational control, the Established status holds and the lever has widened to commerce: Israel halted commercial goods from 13 Oct over Hamas levies on merchants, halving truck entries until a gradual restart on 19 Oct, and activists blocked aid at Kerem Shalom on 22 Oct, so access is now contested by the state, the armed group and domestic politics at once.

items.whyNow: Reporting this week that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for a short, intensive campaign on Iran after the 3 Nov midterms, with three carriers due by early November, turns the current pause into a named strike window. Iran's claimed hits on seven tankers on 21–22 Oct and its threat to extend the fight to US bases kept Brent near $113 and Gulf-to-Asia freight above five times prewar, directly raising costs on Singapore's energy and shipping routes.
changes: 22 Oct: The IRGC claimed seven tankers hit overnight, four during ship-to-ship transfers in the northern Gulf and three by mines west of the strait, none independently confirmed and with no matching UKMTO reports; Trump called the hits 'fake', a CENTCOM spokesperson said lanes are clear and 95% of vessels get through, the IRGC threatened US bases if Washington helps tankers use other routes, and Brent rose about 4% to $113 (Al Jazeera, gCaptain, CBS live).

21 Oct: The New York Times reported US and Israeli plans for a short, intensive campaign on Iranian energy, nuclear, missile and drone targets after the midterms, with three US carriers in place by early November; the FT reported Trump blocked an Israeli strike planned for around 10 Oct, which senior IDF officials denied was ever planned; Araghchi said indirect talks via Pakistan and Qatar continue, and Netanyahu vowed to bring down the regime (Open/NYT, Ynetnews, CBS live, Times of Israel).

20 Oct: Security chief Rezaei told Pakistan's army chief Munir that no enriched uranium will leave Iran, and Ghalibaf listed seven conditions for reopening Hormuz, including an end to the US port blockade; the IMO's chief warned Iran 'still has mines', and Bloomberg found at least 5 of 23 attacks on 1–14 Oct struck engine rooms (Times of Israel, Critical Threats).

19 Oct: Defence Secretary Hegseth met Netanyahu and Defence Minister Katz at Ovda air base in an unannounced visit reported to cover a possible resumption of major combat, a day after Trump endorsed Netanyahu; Netanyahu said 'we have a job to finish' (The National).

18 Oct: Two unknown projectiles hit a tug northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE, injuring one person, in an attack Critical Threats assesses Iran likely carried out, and US embassies across the region issued new security warnings (Critical Threats, CBS live).

17 Oct: Iran claimed two supertankers struck mines, which the JMIC said had 'no substantiation'; on 16 Oct two tankers were hit 68–78 nm northeast of al-Jubail, one by an RPG from a likely IRGC fast attack craft, and UKMTO counted 12 attacks in the week to 16 Oct, one vessel lost (gCaptain, Critical Threats).

history.note: Baseline: Hormuz crisis, direct Singapore exposure.

timeline.text: After Iranian strikes on vessels collapsed the June ceasefire, US Central Command resumed its naval blockade of Iranian ports and struck Iranian anti-shipping targets near Hormuz.

After US strikes on Iranian coastal radars killed 11 people and the IRGC fired anti-ship ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer, CENTCOM destroyed or disabled three Iranian tankers, the Downy, Stark 1 and Kylo.

An Iranian anti-ship cruise missile struck a non-Navy vessel carrying a Marine battalion landing team in the Strait of Hormuz, injuring eight Marines, an attack the Pentagon did not announce until NBC News reported it two weeks later.

Trump publicly rejected Iran's seven-day plan after the Wall Street Journal reported he expects to resume bombing after the November midterms, and the next day the IRGC claimed a second US underwater drone captured in the strait, which CENTCOM called 'clearly desperate'.

Qatar delivered the US reply to Iran's seven-day Hormuz plan as Trump said a decision to strike or deal was coming 'very soon', unknown projectiles hit four tankers in the strait over three days and the last US troops left Iraq.

Trump pledged no attack on Iran before the 3 November midterms while keeping the blockade, after reports that the Pentagon was preparing options to resume major combat, and a tanker caught fire off Fujairah.

The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank after a projectile hit in the Strait of Hormuz the previous day, one of two ships lost within a day, as security data showed at least ten vessels attacked since 11 October.

The IRGC claimed seven tankers hit overnight in and near the Strait of Hormuz, which Trump called fake and no maritime agency confirmed, a day after the New York Times reported US and Israeli plans for a short, intensive strike campaign on Iran after the 3 November midterms.

text: Long-range strike versus integrated air and missile defence (Established · Contested) remains latent but is now scheduled rather than hypothetical: Critical Threats recorded no US or partner strike on Iran from 17 to 21 Oct, yet the New York Times reported on 21 Oct a planned short, intensive campaign after 3 Nov, following Hegseth's 19 Oct meeting with Netanyahu. Earlier strikes straining US interceptor stocks keep the defence side of the contest the weaker one. timeline.text: The United States, Israel and Lebanon signed a US-brokered Trilateral Framework tying phased Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament and creating a trilateral military coordination group.
Lebanese army troops deployed in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, the first of three US-supervised pilot zones, after Israeli forces pulled back from the village.
Israel detonated about 1,100 tonnes of explosives to destroy Hezbollah tunnels under Ali al-Taher ridge and declared its south Lebanon security zone complete.

Hezbollah launched an explosive drone at Israeli troops inside the security zone overnight without causing casualties, the Israeli air force struck drone and anti-tank launch sites across nine southern localities in response, and Qassem told a Nasrallah-anniversary crowd that resistance continues until full expulsion and that Israel must first liberate the south before any dialogue.

Salam asked Rubio in Washington for a withdrawal timeline and a credible verification mechanism and was told the framework is the only path to a durable peace, while the Israeli army levelled much of Mansouri in a mass detonation it said destroyed 600 infrastructure sites and eight tunnels.

EU foreign ministers approved a civilian and military mission of about 150 personnel to train Lebanese forces in border security and counter-drone work as UNIFIL prepares to leave at the end of the year.

Hezbollah publicly claimed a half-tonne explosives shipment seized by Lebanese security forces at Dahr al-Baidar, saying it was meant for use against Israel, a day after Israel's defence minister threatened to seize Nabatieh if Hezbollah joins an Iranian attack.

Two days of US-hosted Lebanon–Israel military talks at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa ended without a breakthrough, with Israel rejecting Lebanon's demand for third-party verification of its army's operations.

text: On border-zone security versus rocket, drone and dispersed-launch threats, the Established and Contested status is borne out only on the Israeli side: no Hezbollah fire was reported between 16 and 22 Oct, while Israeli armour pushed toward Kfar Shuba on 16 Oct and Habbariyeh on 22 Oct, beyond the zone it declared complete, and an Israeli official claimed on 21 Oct that Hezbollah is rebuilding launch capacity in Beirut and the south (single source), so the threat being guarded against is latent rather than active. On precision strike versus escalation control, the contest persists: Israeli fire on 16 and 22 Oct remained area shelling, demolitions and occasional air strikes rather than targeted killings, and Aoun's 22 Oct warning tied escalation risk to a possible Iran round rather than to the border itself.

On ceasefire monitoring versus armed-group reconstitution, the trigger has moved from monitoring failure to internal confrontation: a judge summoned two Hezbollah officials on 20 Oct, the army deployed in Dahiyeh on 17 Oct after gunmen surrounded police, and the Tampa talks ended on 21 Oct with Israel refusing third-party verification, so the Lebanese state, not an external monitor, now carries enforcement.

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.

The first UNCLOS conciliation session in Singapore (14–16 September) closed with Cambodia tabling three settlement options and Thailand insisting a maritime boundary be delimited before any resource sharing; a second meeting was set for The Hague on 14–18 October.
Cambodia formally protested a Buddha statue that Thai troops and monks placed on 18 September at Phnom Beng in Anlong Veng, calling it a fait accompli on occupied land.

Prak Sokhonn told the UN General Assembly that the conflict had seriously eroded trust, that over 20,000 Cambodians still cannot return home, that Thailand should implement the December agreements and resume Joint Boundary Commission demarcation, and that the Charter sets no separate standard for powerful states.

Hun Manet said the United States had asked Thailand to stop escalatory actions and encroachment on Cambodian territory, and Thailand's foreign ministry denied it the same day, conditioning any boundary commission meeting on a border secure from landmines and transnational crime.

The second UNCLOS conciliation meeting opened at the Peace Palace in The Hague as Cambodia and Thailand clashed at the UNHCR Executive Committee in Geneva over the more than 20,000 Cambodians Phnom Penh says cannot return home.

The Hague conciliation round closed with the first agreed confidence-building measures (a direct channel between the two navies among them, by Thailand's account), while the Commission noted earlier measures were unimplemented and set a third meeting in Kuala Lumpur for 24–27 November.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving status is borne out on the ground: no exchange of fire, drone crossing or new mine casualty was reported from 9 to 22 Oct, and on 22 Oct Thailand's defence ministry still rated the border at Level 1.5. The argument has moved to the 2025 record instead, with the Thai army on 22 Oct justifying past strikes at Preah Vihear as self-defence, so incident management now depends on restraint over narratives as much as over fire. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger has not fired: two Vietnamese officers joined the ASEAN Observer Team on 17 Oct (single source), but the Thai army's 15 Oct claim that three Sa Kaeo areas need Thai security controls shows local consolidation continuing beyond what observers can reverse.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status is contradicted. The Hague Commission produced the first agreed package on 18 Oct, including a navy-to-navy channel, yet Thailand framed it on 22 Oct as a test of Cambodian sincerity and both sides traded Preah Vihear accusations within four days, so the process restrains conduct at sea more than signalling ashore. Adaptability stays Low.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger status holds but pressure has moved sideways rather than up: no US boat strike has been reported since 4 Oct, and Washington instead extended its lawfare template to Cuba through Florida's 19 Oct arrest warrant for Raúl Castro, which Venezuela's ruling PSUV condemned on 21 Oct. Legitimacy is contested through procedure and mobilisation rather than force. Adaptability stays Medium: the transferable lesson is in sequencing legal, sanctions and institutional levers, not in new military methods.

timeline.text: China Coast Guard cutter 21585 rammed fisheries vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat 54 nautical miles off Palawan while it refuelled fishermen, damaging its railings; no injuries.

Three PLAN warships, including two Type 022 missile boats, and five China Coast Guard cutters intercepted the MV Lapu-Lapu resupply run about 60 nautical miles from Second Thomas Shoal, a warship radioed that it would take 'compulsory measures' and the mission was suspended, the first blocked run since the July 2024 understanding.

The PLA Southern Theater Command and the China Coast Guard drilled boarding, forced towing and expulsion around Scarborough Shoal with a frigate, corvette, replenishment ship, KJ-500 and the WZ-7 drone 'in response to the acts made by certain countries', while the US ambassador in Manila condemned the 24 September blocking and China's embassy told Washington to 'stop fanning the flames'.

A China Coast Guard cutter trained its water cannon on BRP Cabra during a medical evacuation from BRP Sierra Madre, forcing a small-boat transfer four nautical miles off the reef that delayed the mission by nearly ten hours, while a PLA Navy frigate stood nearby.

Chinese maritime militia vessel 9622 deployed 22 sampans around Philippine-held Kota Island, one within about 250 metres of the shore, and its master encircled the Philippine response boats and claimed the area as Chinese before all the vessels left.

Defence Secretary Teodoro said direct military communication with China would stay suspended until Beijing drops its claims and 'predatory activities', after the Chinese embassy called the cutoff 'reckless and irresponsible' and the armed forces backed him.

The Philippine foreign ministry summoned Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan over his 15 October remark that China 'may easily win' if it used force, calling it provocative and unacceptable, as senators filed a resolution to expel him.

The armed forces completed a rotation-and-resupply run to BRP Sierra Madre without incident, the first since the 24 September interception, while China's coast guard said it had approved and monitored the delivery and Manila denied seeking any permission; the same day PLA Navy ships shadowed USS Charleston near Sabina Shoal.

text: On grey-zone maritime coercion versus presence and resilience, the Established · Contested status is borne out, but the contest shifted from physical blocking to narrative: after the 24 Sep interception and the 8 Oct water-cannon medevac, the 20 Oct resupply went through without incident, and on 21 Oct the coast guard spokesman claimed Beijing had 'approved' and verified it, which the AFP called an invention on 22 Oct. Presence was sustained, yet each run now carries a competing legal record, while the 15-19 Oct ambassador row and the suspended military channel leave little to manage a failed run. On maritime domain awareness versus ambiguous attribution, the Rising status holds: the Navy published a weekly count on 21 Oct of 31 Chinese ships (23 coast guard, 8 PLAN) for 13-19 Oct, and the PLA publicised its own tracking of USS Charleston at Sabina Shoal on 20 Oct, so both sides now use disclosure as a tool.

On distributed maritime posture versus force protection, the Rising · Contested rating is supported: small garrisons on Kota and Lawak pushed militia boats out between 9 and 15 Oct, but seven Chinese ships at Pag-asa in the week to 19 Oct show how thinly held outposts stay crowded. timeline.text: China suspended Japanese seafood imports and warned its citizens against travel to Japan in retaliation for Prime Minister Takaichi's 7 November Diet remark that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could threaten Japan's survival.
China's Commerce Ministry banned exports of dual-use items, including rare earths and magnets, to Japanese military end-users.

Indian destroyer INS Kolkata and Pakistani patrol vessel PNS Hunain collide in the North Arabian Sea during Pakistan's SEASPARK-26 exercise, the first physical military incident since May 2025; each side summons the other's charge d'affaires the next day and India later rejects Pakistan's account as 'the usual prevarication'.

A day after the Indian Army said it had killed Pahalgam-linked LeT commander Hashim Moosa in Budgam, Pakistan's army spokesman presented a man of the same name alive in Rawalpindi, called the claim a 'false flag' and warned of 'very harsh retribution'.

India's Border Security Force shoots dead two Pakistani men on the Punjab border, which India calls an infiltration attempt and Pakistan an unprovoked killing of villagers, and each side summons the other's envoy the next day.

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government in Naypyitaw, and on 21 April offers armed groups peace talks with a 100-day deadline that the KNU, CNF and NUG reject.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.

Three junta jets bomb the National Unity Government's regional command near Kyaikto, killing at least six including Air Force defector Nay Win Aung, as the Arakan Army repels a two-week junta attempt on the Maei pass at Mindon, Malaysia sets 29 Sep to begin deporting Myanmar migrants, Myanmar recalls its ambassador to Thailand, a Delhi court lets the foreign drone trainers leave India and an MNDAA delegation opens Chinese-pressed talks in Naypyidaw.

A junta fighter jet drops two bombs on the main wholesale market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, at about noon, killing at least 33 people and wounding 36 by the Arakan Army's and a senior rescue official's count, the deadliest strike in Rakhine since the December 2025 hospital bombing, with no comment from the military.

Junta warships, artillery and aircraft begin a week of failed landing attempts on Ngapyi Island opposite the Shwe Min Gan naval base near Sittwe, and by 14 October the Arakan Army still holds the island and has taken outposts on the city's edge, by local accounts.

Min Aung Hlaing met Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Putrajaya on a two-day official visit and pledged to take back verified Myanmar nationals as soon as possible, with a second phase of 3,524 returns awaiting a date.

The Arakan Army takes two outposts near Kyarmathauk, about four miles north of the junta's Regional Operations Command in Sittwe, and fights for an engineering battalion there as the air force strikes its positions, by an AA source.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status is borne out: regime aircraft killed 16 civilians in Magway, Mandalay and Chin in one day reported on 20 Oct, six women in Budalin on 20 Oct and two people in Pauktaw on 20 Oct, yet airpower has not stopped the Arakan Army taking outposts four miles from the Sittwe command on 16 Oct (AA-sourced, unverified) after the 7–14 Oct Ngapyi landings failed. Ground gains still run against the regime in Rakhine, while elsewhere it advances slowly on four fronts in southern Chin (single source). On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is reinforced from the state side: Myanmar Now attributed the 20 Oct toll to gyrocopters and kamikaze drones alongside jets, showing the regime adding cheap aerial platforms to its strike mix as the AA did with drones against landing craft on 8–9 Oct.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status holds: TNLA and MNDAA upgraded Chinese border gates (16 Oct), a TNLA-backed unit defected in Kyaukme (single source), and US talks in Tokyo and Sasakawa's 20 Oct visit show outsiders dealing with Naypyitaw over corridors and minerals. Adaptability stays High.

items.whyNow: Houthi strikes reached Dammam airport and the Shaybah oilfield on 21 Oct, on the Gulf side of Saudi Arabia, prompting Aramco to evacuate headquarters staff and the US to order diplomats out, while the UK's Typhoon deployment on 20 Oct shows outside air forces being drawn in to plug a stretched Saudi defence. With Hormuz also under attack, Saudi energy and its Red Sea export bypass, on which Singapore-bound flows depend, are inside the fight.
changes: 22 Oct: Saudi authorities raised the Dammam airport toll to two dead and eight injured and reopened the airport; the Houthis claimed strikes on the Saudi Defence Ministry in Riyadh and Aramco at Yanbu (unconfirmed), the coalition said it intercepted four more drones over Riyadh and Medina, and the UN said nearly 260,000 Yemenis have been displaced since August, about half in Taiz (Ynetnews, CBS live, Al Jazeera).

21 Oct: A Houthi attack on King Fahd airport in Dammam and drone debris at the Shaybah oilfield each killed two people, Aramco ordered staff out of its headquarters and the US ordered non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia; the Houthis hit Aden airport and al-Rayyan airport in Mukalla, and Iraq closed the al-Sheeb crossing with Iran and reportedly ordered Houthi offices shut, which Baghdad's spokesman denied exist (The National, Al-Monitor, Critical Threats).

20 Oct: Britain said RAF Typhoons will fly defensive counter-air missions over Saudi cities and infrastructure and extended air-to-air refuelling for Saudi operations; Saudi defences intercepted a missile and a drone aimed at Riyadh, and government forces and Houthis contested Jabal Han above Taiz (Al Jazeera, Critical Threats).

19 Oct: Three Houthi ballistic missiles hit the al-Alam training camp in Shabwa, killing at least 53 per the local authority (later reports said 73), and Egypt's parliament delayed for a second day a vote on military support for Saudi Arabia, now set for 26 Oct (Al Jazeera, The National).

18 Oct: A US official told the WSJ that Saudi forces intercept about 90% of Houthi attacks but that over half target undefended sites; Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman met UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed after reports the UAE will resume paying government-aligned forces, and Sisi offered defensive military aid (Critical Threats).

17 Oct: A Saudi AH-6i helicopter crashed over Najran, killing both pilots; Riyadh cited a malfunction while an OSINT analyst suggested a Houthi surface-to-air missile (single source); Saudi defences intercepted three drones and two ballistic missiles, a day after two Houthi missiles hit Aden airport (Critical Threats).

timeline.text: The Houthis declare a naval and air blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to a strike on Sanaa airport, ending four years of relative calm under the 2022 truce.

The US-led coalition ended its 12-year mission in Iraq as the last US troops left, while Iraqi militias refused to disarm and a new breakaway militia with Iranian support was reported.

A Houthi missile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's King Khalid airport, killing 12 people and wounding 309 by Saudi count, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade, and the airport was shut.

Houthi missiles hit the presidential palace complex in Aden for the first time in this conflict, killing five people by the health minister's count, as the coalition reported 20 attacks on Riyadh airport in October.
Three Houthi ballistic missiles hit the al-Alam training camp for new security recruits in Shabwa, killing at least 53 people by the local authority's count.
A Houthi attack on Dammam's King Fahd airport killed two people and drone debris at the Shaybah oilfield killed two more, as the US ordered non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia.

text: Long-range attack versus layered protection is borne out as Rising · Contested and still favours the attacker: Houthi strikes reached Dammam airport and the Shaybah oilfield on 21 Oct, killing four, and three ballistic missiles killed at least 53 recruits in Shabwa on 19 Oct. A US official's claim on 18 Oct that Saudi defences stop about 90% of attacks while over half target undefended sites shows the attacker adapting to the defender's prioritisation, and the defender's answer is to borrow capacity, with British Typhoons committed to defensive patrols on 20 Oct. Maritime disruption versus route resilience is Established · Contested on land rather than at sea: no Houthi attack on merchant shipping appeared in the fortnight, while the fight for the Red Sea shore and Taiz continued, with government forces retaking Dhubab airport on 15 Oct and Jabal Han contested on 20 Oct.

Regional basing versus militia targeting is borne out in a new form: the US ordered non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia on 21 Oct, and Iraq closed a border crossing with Iran the same day amid reported US pressure. Adaptability is High on the first topic and Medium on the other two.
